newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: World Bank economist mixed on Bangladesh economy.
newsitem.headline: World Bank economist mixed on Bangladesh economy.

text.p: The World Bank painted a mixed picture of Bangladesh's economy on Thursday, praising its steady macro-economic growth under the new government but noting infrastructure remained poor and financial reforms slow.

"Bangladesh's macroeconomy is not in crisis, rather it is well balanced. (The) growth rate is not below standard, (forex) reserve is roughly satisfactory and inflation is low," said John Williamson, the World Bank's chief economist for South Asia.
Though the government's attitude towards reforms was "positive," several key areas needed special attention, Williamson said to reporters after a meeting of international donors here.

"Savings have been rising but still, it is only 13 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP). To sustain the economic upliftment and to generate rapid growth, the country needs the savings rate to rise faster," he said.

The "economy will not be dynamic without further export earnings," he said, referring to the country's potentially huge garments industry. Annual exports from a 2,600-firm garment industry was about $2.5 billion out of total annual exports worth about $4.5 billion.
"Bangldesh can reap fruits from its dynamic neighbouring countries, particularly from the East Asian nations," Williamson said.
"The country is trying to learn from their success stories, and this is very encouraging."
He emphasized the importance of building infrastructure including roads, transportation, power, telecommunications and energy.
But he criticised Bangladesh's industrial policy for not being supportive like that of East Asian countries.

"The private sector should be the main engine for economic development," he said. "But bureaucracy is an impediment to the path of private sector development. I am hesitant to recommend the industrial policy as (the) best one." Williamson said financial sector reforms were also a major problem. "Overdue (unpaid loans are) very high in commercial banks. Even some of them are in danger," he said.
Government officials said private and public companies had defaulted on about $3.5 billion in bank loans.

Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's government has promised sweeping reforms since taking over in June, but analysts doubt she can implement them steadfastly under looming threats of unrest from the opposition. Williamson told a reporter "political stability was very important for attaining and sustaining development."
